article_text:
Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace have begun their international press tour to promote their movie, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping .

The duo kicked things off in Sydney, the home country of Zada, who plays young Haymitch Abernathy.

Grace will play tribute Maysilee Donner in the film, set for U.S. release on November 20, 2026.

RELATED: Everything We Know About The ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Movie So Far

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is directed by Francis Lawrence from a screenplay by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie, based on the adaptation and novel by Suzanne Collins.

The film follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Zada) from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes.

Set in the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games , the story follows Haymitch into the arena, where he forms an unlikely alliance with fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Grace) and joins a coalition determined to challenge the Capitol’s control under President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

As the competition unfolds, Haymitch risks everything to take down the Games from within the arena — setting in motion the rebellion that will change Panem forever.

The cast includes Joseph Zada, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Ben Wang. Other actors featured include Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, and Kelvin Harrison Jr.

article_text:
ザ・ノース・フェイス（THE NORTH FACE）の創業60周年を記念したアートエキシビション「EXPLORING WITH NATURE｜自然とともに探求すること」が、11月9日（月）まで、京都のTHE NORTH FACE STANDARD 京都で開催されている。

1966年の創業以来、自然への敬意と探求心をブランドの理念に掲げてきたザ・ノース・フェイス。本展では、自然と人間の関係をテーマに、異なる領域で活動する4名のアーティストの作品を紹介する。

参加するのは、アメリカを拠点に自然現象を取り入れた作品を制作するサム・フォールズ、1960年代末に登場した「もの派」の主要作家である菅木志雄、写真やフィールドレコーディングを通して人間と非人間、場所の記憶を探る濵本奏、そして日本の伝統技法「乾漆」を用いて生命や自然の神秘を表現する小梛真弓の4名。

石や木、金属と空間の関係を問い続ける菅の実践から、写真、音、漆といった多様なメディアを通じた表現まで、それぞれの作品は自然を単なる鑑賞対象ではなく、人間と関わり合う存在として捉えている。

本展が問いかけるのは、未知の場所へ踏み出すことだけではない「探求」のあり方だ。身近な自然の変化に目を向け、人間もまた自然の一部であることを再認識する。アウトドアブランドの理念と現代アートの実践が交差する展覧会となる。

Donald Insall, doyen of conservation architects, who has died aged 100, was very clear about the distinction between preserving buildings and conserving them. “Preservation,” he pronounced, “is what you do for marmalade.” Though Insall could see the value of preservation, he was an adroit conservationist rather than a stodgy marmalade maker, always seeing how historic buildings could be revived and put to new uses.

Marshalling teams of architects, craftsmen and builders, he brought Windsor Castle back from the brink following the devastating “ annus horribilis ” fire of 1992. The exacting rescue scheme encompassed a range of strategies, from complete restoration to renewal in spirit. “As well as keeping things as they were, or putting them back as one thinks they were – which is chancy and not the main aim – we had to find new solutions to parts that had been irreparably destroyed,” Insall told Country Life in 2018.

Other high-profile projects included the renovation of Kelmscott Manor, the Oxfordshire country home of the writer, designer and socialist William Morris, following its acquisition by the Society of Antiquaries in 1961, and the restoration of Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire, Robert Adam’s Palladian masterpiece, now in the care of the National Trust. “Kedleston was our first big job,” Insall recalled. “I used to take a scooter on the train, hop off at Derby and go to the hall, where I was met by the butler and the dogs. Once or twice, Lord Scarsdale, the owner, came on the back of the scooter for a ride around the estate.”

Insall was also involved in the lengthy rebuilding of Wotton House in Buckinghamshire, which had previously been remodelled by John Soane following a fire in 1820. Derelict and teetering on the brink of destruction, it was bought in 1957 by the enterprising Elaine Brunner, daughter of King George V’s valet, who had first arrived there, chauffeured by an antique dealer friend, to scavenge columns to adorn her swimming pool and then embarked on a decades-long programme of restoration.

Commissioned by custodians of the country’s most significant historic buildings, from town halls to royal palaces, Insall changed the scope and ambition of conservation practice, shaping pioneering approaches to heritage management at a time when historic buildings were widely seen as impediments to progress rather than assets to be cherished. In deftly addressing issues of heritage, sustainability and contemporary use, his approach has a renewed resonance and relevance. When Insall once worked for the College of Arms, he was granted a personal coat of arms. Aptly, he chose the motto “Bring Forth the Best”.

The son of Phyllis (nee Hill) and William Insall, he was born in Bristol into a family of long established manufacturers of traditional luggage, such as trunks, cricket bags and portmanteaux. He attended Bristol grammar school, and his interest in architecture was piqued when his father commissioned and built a new family home at Henleaze, in the north of the city. During the blitz, Insall witnessed the wartime destruction of Bristol’s ancient churches and historic buildings, and in 1942 started architectural studies at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture . He saw wartime service from 1944 in the Coldstream Guards, completing his education after being demobbed in 1948.

Insall studied civic design in London at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the RA’s School of Planning. In 1951 he was a Lethaby scholar with the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, the organisation founded by William Morris in 1877 in response to the activities of Victorian architects, whose misconceived enthusiasm for restoration often caused calamitous damage. As a Lethaby scholar, Insall worked with and learned from an array of traditional craftsmen, including thatchers and lime plasterers, going on to spend 18 months measuring and surveying Winchester college for the medieval historian John Harvey .

It proved a formative education in which he got to know and understand historic buildings from different periods. He claimed to have no favourites. “I love them all,” he said, relishing how social change was reflected in architecture. “It’s all part of a lively continuity.” What also mattered to him was not just the quality of individual buildings, but their wider contextual relationships with streets, towns and cities. The role of conservation architects was, Insall believed, to help make “every place to be truly more itself”.

Insall initially joined Phillimore and Jenkins, a London-based practice specialising in the restoration of country houses in the greatly altered postwar milieu. In 1958, together with a fellow Lethaby scholar, Peter Locke, he founded Donald Insall Associates, working from the kitchen table in his flat in Belgravia. His father and then his wife, Libby (nee Moss), a lawyer, whom he married in 1964, did the accounts. From these tentative beginnings, the practice is now over 100 strong, operating out of eight offices across England and Wales.

With modernism then in the ascendancy, it was a bleak time for historic buildings. Country houses that did not find a saviour were all too often demolished, as were urban swathes of Victorian and Georgian terraces. While conservation fired Insall’s imagination, taking an interest in old houses was regarded as perplexingly antiquarian, as he recounted to Country Life. “Nice to meet you, but when will your father be coming?” asked the builder on one early job.

Insall’s 1968 study of Chester was a landmark for urban conservation and town planning. Undertaken as a part of a government pilot project surveying four historic towns (the others were Bath, Chichester and York), it recognised for the first time the importance of groups of structures with historic or architectural value. Insall and his team “crawled in overalls” over some 400 buildings, evaluating their merits and advocating that the best ones should be retained.

This led to his appointment as conservation consultant for Chester, and, ultimately, to the establishment of municipal conservation officers in local councils across the country. It also helped formulate many of the principles that underpin today’s conservation management plans and historic building appraisals.

Over time, Insall became a driving force in the workings of the Ancient Monuments Board and the Historic Buildings Council for England. There he befriended the architectural historian John Summerson, and the historians and conservation activists Nikolaus Pevsner and John Betjeman. These liaisons seeded the formation of English Heritage in 1984, of which Insall was a founding commissioner.

Conservation techniques are continually evolving and Insall kept abreast of developments. In the decade-long restoration of Westminster Hall completed in 2020, for instance, nanolime (nano-sized particles of calcium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol) was used to consolidate weathered limestone, and latex poultices employed to remove staining. Insall was also a thoughtful writer, summarising his philosophy, principles and practice in Living Buildings (2008), reprinted a decade later with a foreword by the then Prince of Wales.

For the last three years, Insall projects have won the Europa Nostra award, Europe’s highest accolade for heritage conservation: for the restoration of Westminster Hall (2024), the saving from dereliction of the 18th-century Camellia House at Wentworth Woodhouse, in South Yorkshire (2025) and the revitalisation of Rochdale’s imposing neo-Gothic Town Hall (2026).

Whether resplendent in elegant tweed suits on Instagram, commuting to the office on a BMW 750 motorbike, or vertiginously face to face with Nelson at the top of his column, Insall cultivated a suavely swashbuckling persona, laced with charm and humour. Though he retired as practice chairman in 1998, he continued to work as a consultant until his death.

“Buildings are so very much like people,” he observed. “They all have their own characters, their own strengths and weaknesses, their own message, their own background in terms of the influences that have made them. People change throughout their lives – so does a building.”

Insall was knighted in 2010. He is survived by Libby and their three children, Robert, Christopher and Hilary.

Born in Plymouth, Devon, in 1993, Henry Slade is a centre for Exeter Chiefs and England. He came up through the Exeter Chiefs academy, making his senior debut for the club in 2012, and has since earned more than 75 caps for England. He lifted the Champions Cup and won the Premiership title and the Six Nations in successive weekends in 2020. At 18, he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes – a condition his father, John, also lives with – and he has since launched the Tackle Diabetes campaign, in partnership with the pharmaceutical company Sanofi, to raise awareness of the signs and symptoms of the disease and the value of early detection. He lives near Exeter with his wife and three daughters. For more information about early detection, visit testfortype1.com

Henry (on left)

This was taken after my first game for England’s under-18s. Wearing the shirt was a cool moment, but I was feeling knackered and giving a nervous smile. I was a bit of a shy kid back then.

A few months later, I was diagnosed with diabetes. I was 18 and doing my A-levels. There was no real sign – I was healthy and didn’t have any of the typical symptoms, such as losing loads of weight, frequent urination or being thirsty. I just woke up and felt really bad one day. Actually, it was the only day I ever had off school – Mum and Dad never used to let me have a sick day as they needed to go to work. My mate was ill, too, but I didn’t realise he’d been admitted to hospital with diabetic ketoacidosis. He was back at school the next week and told us he’d been diagnosed with diabetes – he’d brought in a finger-prick test we could all try. I did mine and my blood glucose levels were high. I had another test at the GP that confirmed the diagnosis. It was a shock, but I was lucky we detected it early.

I’d grown up seeing my dad live with diabetes, so my diagnosis wasn’t as upsetting as it might be for other people. Throughout my childhood, I’d always seen Dad do triathlons and windsurfing. There were definite challenges, though – I was a teenager and had started going out and drinking with mates, and I was also a sportsman. It took a lot of getting used to, constantly thinking about what food and drink I was putting in my body so I could get my blood glucose levels right. Has it inhibited me in a game? I’ve only needed to eat a load of Jelly Babies to avoid a hypo (low blood sugar) before playing a few times. If anything, I like to focus on the positive side to type 1 diabetes: it’s made me so resilient and very conscious of my body and what it needs.

As a child, I did certain things to feel OK – small rituals to make sure my friends and family were safe. I now know that was obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). I’m a bit better now, but some rituals I can’t quite kick. Like, if I pick something up, I need to put my little finger down first, and there’s a certain way I like to turn off a light switch. In a strange way, OCD and type 1 diabetes aren’t a bad combination – both need controlling 24/7, and the hypervigilance that comes with OCD has actually made me very good at managing my levels. At the minute, I’m obsessed with my glucose data, which is obviously important because it’s my health – but it’s also occasionally annoying.

Throughout it all, it’s been so reassuring to have Dad next to me, someone who understands completely. Dad’s very particular. He knows what he likes, and what he doesn’t. He is strong-willed, but I haven’t argued with him since I was a teenager. We’d have some small fallouts, and some louder ones. Mainly about going to parties. The day I passed my driving test, my mate was having a party in Cornwall and I wanted to drive my friends to it. Dad said no – he didn’t want me to be responsible for four other boys in the car the day I passed. He knew I would be too excited to drive properly. I was angry at the time, but now I’m a dad I’d do the exact same thing.

I’ve probably played 280 times for Chiefs and I reckon Dad’s missed about five games in total. I’m very grateful for everything he has done for me. Along with Mum, he’s given up a lot. They sent us to private school when finances were tight. He gave me every opportunity, but never pushed me to do anything I didn’t want to. He told me anything was possible and has been there every step of the way.

John

I was extremely proud of Henry that day he played for England’s under-18s. I never expected my own child would play at that level. I’d always thought, “Wouldn’t it be great if I could be Jonny Wilkinson’s dad?” That’s why I am smiling from inside out.

When Henry got diagnosed with diabetes, my first thought was, “This is my fault.” I worried he’d inherited it from my genes. It was a little bit traumatic for me to process what had happened, but since then I’ve learned there is a one in 300 chance of developing type 1 diabetes for anyone. If there’s a close family member, then it’s one in 20.

Henry was nine months old when I was diagnosed. One of my biggest fears was that I wouldn’t be able to see him grow older. My eyesight had changed and I was worried I was going blind. That was a heavy time.

As Henry got older, he became a determined kid – very focused. He didn’t like to lose. It’s a competitive spirit that my wife and I have. Henry and I are both quiet, compared with Henry’s mum, who can talk for England. He and I aren’t the loudest in the room, but we have to win.

Even though I could see Henry had a tremendous talent, I was never a pushy parent. You do see mums or dads giving their kid £10 or a Mars bar for scoring a try, but I never did that. Instead, I encouraged him to acknowledge the commitment we were making. At the start of the season, I would hold the chequebook in front of me and say, “Right, I’m going to write this – if you want to drop out halfway through the season, forget it. It’s paid for.” That was the only push – that we were financially locked in for that year. I was also often loud on the touchline. Once, I got sent off by a school in Devon for cheering our side too enthusiastically. What did I shout? Nothing bad, I just loudly encouraged them, as the opposite side was cheating.

Diabetes has definitely bonded us. Henry teaches me, really, because he’s so well controlled. I am 33 years into it now, so my symptoms are very faint, although I did fall asleep after bathing Henry’s daughter a few years ago. I took her into the bedroom to dry her and was just about to put her nappy on when I fell asleep on the floor. I’d been out for 10 minutes. She shouted, “Dada’s asleep!” Thankfully, someone else was at home to take over.

Before every game, I text Henry, saying “best of luck”. I send him some heart emojis and tell him how proud I am. I don’t tend to say it to his face much, as the written word is easier. But I hope he knows that what he has achieved is beyond my wildest dreams.

article_text:
Jessica Lange says she feels her acting career might be “coming to an end,” and that her current film, Long Day’s Journey Into Night , wouldn’t be a bad way to go out.

In an interview with Rolling Stone posted yesterday, Lange addressed a wide range of topics and a look back at her own career when she was asked what roles she’d like to tackle in the future. (Watch the interview below.)

“I actually feel like I’m coming to an end,” said Lange, fresh off a dual role in Ryan Murphy’s American Horror Story 13. ” “And maybe it’s not a bad way to end, you know, the last film being Long Day’s Journey Into Night and playing Mary Tyrone .”

Related Stories

'Long Day's Journey Into Night' Starring Jessica Lange, Ed Harris & Ben Foster Acquired By Quiver

Lange cited the dearth of roles for women and the difficulty in getting projects off the ground as playing factors in her feelings about the future, a subject that figured into her previous Murphy series Feud: Bette and Joan (she played Joan Crawford to Susan Sarandon’s Bette Davis) and also informs a project she’s been hoping to get underway for some time: A Marlene Dietrich biopic.

Watch on Deadline

“We touched on this with Ryan [Murphy]’s project Feud with Joan and Bette about what happens when an actress gets to a certain age and they’re no longer viable,” Lange said. “That was the theme with Bette and Joan, [and] that is a recurrent theme for a lot of women, especially of that period.” She added that the Dietrich project would focus on “what she did, where she moved on from when Hollywood was kind of finished with her.”

Lange said the Dietrich project is one of a couple that have “been in the works for ever and may or may not happen. It doesn’t seem easy to get things made anymore, at least not the kind of films that interest me.”

Long Day’s Journey Into Night , directed by Jonathan Kent and starring Lange, Ed Harris, Ben Foster and Colin Morgan, was filmed in 2022, six years after Kent and Lange did the Eugene O’Neill play on Broadway (Lange won a Tony Award for her performance). The film was released in the U.S. last month.

article_text:
Em "Bond 26", Pattinson vai reeditar sua parceira com o diretor Denis Villeneuve.

O nome é Pattinson. Robert Pattinson . Após meses de especulação, Amazon e MGM finalmente confirmaram o ator britânico como o novo 007 nos cinemas. A informação foi confirmada por meio de um pequeno teaser que apresentou o primeiro vislumbre de Pattinson como James Bond. Assista acima.

Em declaração oficial, Pattinson comemorou a escalação:

“James Bond é um dos personagens mais lendários do cinema, e ser incumbido do papel de 007 é a honra de uma vida. Sou profundamente grato a Denis, Amy, David, Tanya e a todos na Amazon MGM Studios pela confiança em mim. Dizer que este papel é um sonho realizado é pouco. Não poderia estar mais entusiasmado com esta parceria e com o trabalho que temos pela frente com esta equipe fantástica.”

O processo de seleção foi longo, com Pattinson surgindo como o principal candidato apenas nas últimas semanas. Antes, os nomes mais especulados eram os de Callum Turner (da série “Mestres do Ar”), Jack Lowden (da série de espionagem “Slow Horses”) e Josh O’Connor (da série “The Crown”).

Pattinson assume o papel já no próximo filme, que também marca a retomada de sua parceria com o diretor Denis Villeneuve. A dupla vem de uma colaboração recente em “Duna: Parte 3”. Villeneuve participou do processo de escolha e elogiou Pattinson:

“Antes de mais nada, quero expressar minha profunda gratidão aos atores notáveis ​​que se juntaram a nós nesta jornada. Estávamos cercados por talentos extraordinários, mas só pode haver um 007. Estou imensamente feliz em dar as boas-vindas a Robert Pattinson como nosso novo James Bond. Ele possui a alma atemporal do 007 e traz um espírito totalmente novo. Mal posso esperar para começar.”

Além da escolha do novo James Bond, a expectativa agora fica para a escalação de outros personagens clássicos da franquia, como M, Q, Moneypenny e Felix Leiter, além, claro, do próximo vilão e da próxima Bond Girl.

O próximo “007”, chamado por enquanto de “Bond 26”, terá roteiro de Steven Knight, da série “Peaky Blinders”. Tanya Lapointe, Amy Pascal e David Heyman serão os produtores.

Ainda não há data de estreia confirmada para o próximo “007”, com especulações indicando um possível lançamento apenas em 2028.

“It’s really a privilege to be able to play a character that could in any way possibly inspire anyone,” Steinfeld previously told Variety about embodying the beloved comic character. “Kate Bishop is a character that I would have loved to have had growing up — somebody who is completely ambitious, driven and disciplined, and takes it upon herself to do whatever it is she has to do to achieve her goals.”

But this time, the scene continues with Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom appearing, lifting the rubble off Wanda and addressing her, confirming fan speculation that Wanda would return.

“ Avengers: Doomsday ” hits theaters on Dec. 18.

Moments after it emerged that Netflix had gotten rid of Bela Bajaria , it named Peter Rice as her replacement.

Former Disney exec Rice takes the job starting October 26.

Rice will oversee all content at Netflix including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.

Rice’s last full-time job was as Chairman of Walt Disney Television and Chairman of General Entertainment for The Walt Disney Company. He was fired in June 2022 and replaced by Dana Walden.

He was named Head of Ceremonies and Content for the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games in July 2025.

Watch on Deadline

“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across TV and film is deep and broad,” said Ted Sarandos, Co-CEO, Netflix. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives. I’m excited to welcome him to Netflix as Chief Content Officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love.”

Rice, whose name started circulating for the Netflix job last week, is a rare executive with high-level experience in both features and TV having run Fox Searchlight and subsequently the Fox Networks Group and Disney’s television operation. One area he does not have a lot of experience — streaming.

“Netflix has fundamentally changed the way stories are made, shared and experienced around the world,” said Rice. “They’ve shown again and again that they’re willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I’m excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere.”

Since leaving Disney, Rice has been producing movies, most recently The Social Reckoning, which opened last weekend.

Internal Email from Ted Sarandos

Hi everyone, I have an important update to share about our Content leadership. After a phenomenal decade at Netflix, Bela is leaving the company. It’s hard to overstate the impact Bela has had during her time here. From expanding our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports to helping shape the broadening of our content offering around the world. So much of what you see on Netflix today can be traced back to a Bela initiative: Insatiable, Queer Eye, Lupin, You, The Diplomat, WWE, YuYu Hakusho, The Night Agent, Heeramandi: The Diamond Bazaar, Squid Game, Tyson vs Paul, Cien años de soledad, the NFL. She also helped reshape our strategy to focus on fewer, bigger, better movies, championing films like KPop Demon Hunters, The Adventures of Cliff Booth, and Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, as well as bringing award winning films like La Bola Negra and Possible Love to Netflix. A tremendous and diverse range of content (and that’s just a snapshot), bringing joy to our members across so many genres. Bela has built and shaped a truly global Content organization, hiring brilliant people and empowering them to make good decisions. I am incredibly grateful to her for everything she’s done. I know this is a big change in a year that has already had its share. But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world. To help us seize on this moment, I’m excited to share that we’ve hired a new leader. Peter Rice is joining Netflix as our new Chief Content Officer beginning next week. Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across both TV and film is deep and broad. On the film side, running Fox Searchlight, he helped bring beloved fan favorite films like Slumdog Millionaire, Little Miss Sunshine, Sideways and Juno to screens. And more recently, as Chairman of Walt Disney Television, he led one of the most successful television divisions in the world, where he was responsible for a massive breadth and scale of shows ranging from The Simpsons, American Idol ,and Modern Family, to The Bear, and Abbott Elementary, along with ABC News programming and major sporting events such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup Finals. He’s one of the few people in our industry who has ever operated at the quality and scale that we do at Netflix every day. In the last few years, he has turned his attention to creating and has produced films with Alex Garland, Danny Boyle, Chris Rock, Jason Reitman and Aaron Sorkin at Sony and A24. I’ve gotten to know Peter personally over the years, and I’ve always been impressed by his straightforward approach, the depth of his relationships and his exceptional creative and business instincts. Talent should have the best experiences of their life here, and Peter and I both believe that Netflix can and should be the home of the best storytellers in the world. It’s been an eventful series of days here, and I realize we’ve asked you to absorb a lot of news and a lot of information. But we all know change is what we do at Netflix. Greg and I will host a companywide town hall on Wednesday, October 21. I want everyone to hear how we’re thinking about the strategy and our execution amid this week’s changes, and to have a chance to ask questions. It will be informal and mostly Q&A, so please bring your questions about this week’s changes and anything else on your mind. Please join me in thanking Bela, and welcoming Peter to the team. Ted

Soudain

Un film de Ryûsuke Hamaguchi

Avec Virginie Efira, Tao Okamoto, Kyozo Nagatsuka et Kodai Kurosaki

Genre : Drame

Durée : 3h16

Note : Si le téléchargement ne fonctionne pas en cliquant directement sur un lien, veuillez cliquer avec le bouton droit sur ce lien et choisir l'option "Enregistrer la cible du lien sous..." ou "Enregistrer le lien sous..." ou "Télécharger le fichier lié sous..." suivant votre navigateur.

Directrice d'un établissement pour personnes âgées, Marie-Lou tente d'y instaurer une philosophie de soins innovante basée sur l'écoute et la dignité des résidents, malgré la réticence d’une partie de ses équipes. Sa rencontre avec Mari, une metteuse en scène japonaise qui se bat contre un cancer, va bouleverser sa trajectoire. En nouant une amitié profonde, les deux femmes engagent ensemble un combat pour “rendre possible l’impossible”.

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“很多时候，当机构试图与社区建立联系时，他们往往是将艺术家‘空降’到一个本身就已经拥有艺术和文化的空间，”该博物馆前公共实践与社区合作经理兰迪·埃文斯解释道，“我们非常清楚自己的角色，即要避开那种叙事，转而与这些地方原本就在发生的事情展开合作。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "paragraph", "text": "首场工作坊于2024年11月举行，当时展览巡展至黑尔县，奥本大学专注于乡村住房开发的校外建筑项目“乡村工作室”便坐落于此。这些拼布被在当地的多个场馆展出——埃文斯将其称为“拼布小径”——包括乡村工作室的一个项目纽伯恩图书馆、格林斯伯勒的艺术画廊苏马克小屋，以及将展览的历史清算焦点置于前台的安全屋黑人历史博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后，展览巡展至阿拉巴马州弗洛伦斯的“线之方式研讨会”。该研讨会由设计师兼纺织艺术家娜塔莉·查宁创立，2025年的主题聚焦于食物、衣物和庇护所。研讨会还在弗洛伦斯的肯尼迪-道格拉斯艺术中心举办了拼布被制作工作坊。“威灵山拼布制作者的体验之一，就是她们在工作时也会唱歌，”参加了多场线下工作坊的巴洛解释道，“因此歌声此起彼伏，人们分散在这座历史悠久的老宅的各个角落，缝纫、学做女红、了解这个故事。”", "到2026年初，该展览将重返朱尔博物馆，在主展厅获得一个更加长期的展位；正如巴洛所解释的那样，这对于一个策展项目来说是一条不同寻常的轨迹。“大多数时候都是策展部门先开发出一个展览，然后教育部门再作出回应，”她说，“然而，这是一个由‘流动博物馆’最终催生出展览的计划。当你以这种方式工作时，你就能获得更多来自社区心声的输入，从一开始他们就是对话的一部分。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在展厅内，除了展出温妮·麦奎因、伊冯娜·韦尔斯和梅赛德斯·布拉克斯顿的拼布被外，还陈列了朗兹县其他本土艺术家的作品。其中包括国际知名的非主流艺术家比尔·特雷勒的一幅绘画、诺亚·普里福伊生动的立体拼贴画、查理·卢卡斯的一件雕塑，以及一张来自朗兹县自由组织的 海报。通过将常设收藏中的作品与社区的拼布被并置，展览不仅强调了该地区艺术形式的多样性，也凸显了这些实践公开的政治属性；例如，朗兹县自由组织曾在极端暴力和恐吓的时期为赋权黑人选民而战。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不久后，该展览成为了奥本大学各专业课程参观的焦点，吸引了艺术史、哲学、历史甚至是工程学专业的学生。“许多在阿拉巴马州出生的学生，他们所在的社区可能没有博物馆，”该馆的传播总监夏洛特·亨德里克斯（Charlotte Hendrix）解释道，“朱尔美术馆可能是他们第一次走进一个可能会让人感到有距离感的空间；他们可能会觉得自己必须对艺术了解很多。当学生们亲身参与到这个过程中时，就主动、投入的学习而言，这真的是无与伦比的体验。”", "translated": true}]

Feature

Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

In a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church, a group of women is sewing the legacies of enslaved people into their quilts.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity and Activism at The Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University (photo Mike Cortez, all images courtesy The Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art)

AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project . The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

“A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross ; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez)

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

The first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity and Activism at The Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University (photo Mike Cortez)

By early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she says. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”

Within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

The exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”

EXCLUSIVE: The Chris Rock directed dramedy, Misty Green , from A24 will hit Netflix on Nov. 9.

While A24’s pay-one output deal with HBO Max, Rock’s first directorial in 12 years lands at Netflix given his long-running relationship with the streamer on its comedy specials.

Misty Green , which made its world premiere at TIFF, is currently playing in limited theaters nationwide.

Rock wrote, directed, and produced the film, and stars alongside Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, and Topher Grace. The pic follows Eleazar as Misty, a once-promising actress who is fighting for a second act.

The actress’ work has earned a Toronto International Film Festival Tribute Award, the Hamptons Film Festival Breakthrough Performer Award, the Mill Valley Film Festival Spotlight Award, and the Middleburg Film Festival Breakthrough Actor Award. She was also named one of Newport Film Festival x Variety’s “10 Actors to Watch” and will receive a Breakthrough Award at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival later this month.

Deadline Chief Film Critic Pete Hammond praised Eleazar in Misty Green , writing that the movie is “all lifted way up high by Eleazar, who makes this all worth the ticket. She’s mesmerizing in one of the best performances by an actress this year. You believe her; you may even know her.”

Misty Green is produced by incoming Netflix Content Boss Peter Rice, Rock, David Worthen Brooks, Victoria Thomas.

article_text:
Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky , chronicling the making of the 1976 classic Rocky , is set to open the Cairo International Film Festival’s 47th edition in November.

In a timely connection, the choice of film ties in with the fact that Cairo, which is Egypt ‘s oldest film festival, also is marking the 50th anniversary of its creation in 1976, even if it is only at its 47th edition.

Related Stories

‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Peter Farrelly’s Sensational Biopic Of The Making Of Stallone’s Classic Is Just As Inspiring As The Original Movie – Toronto Film Festival

‘I Play Rocky’s Peter Farrelly Talks Why The Making Of ‘Rocky’ Was The Next Real-Life Story He Wanted To Take A Swing At – Toronto Studio

The biopic stars Anthony Ippolito in the role of a young Sylvester Stallone as he struggles to establish himself in Hollywood and bring his passion project Rocky to the big screen, while retaining his place in the lead role.

I Play Rocky world premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September, where it was first runner-up for the People’s Choice Award .

Watch on Deadline

It went on to win the Audience Award in the Galas & Special Presentations section at the Vancouver Film Festival and the Audience Choice Award for Best Feature Film at Canada’s Cinéfest Sudbury Film Festival.

The film also was selected for a surprise screening at the BFI London Film Festival and featured at the Rome, Zurich, and Chicago film festivals, as well as AFI FEST, where it screened in the Red Carpet Premieres section.

RELATED: ‘I Play Rocky’ Trailer: “Do You Believe In Me…Or Not?”; The Ultimate Underdog Story Looks A Knockout

“By selecting I Play Rocky as its opening film, CIFF continues its commitment to showcasing cinema that combines artistic merit with audience appeal, while turning the spotlight on the filmmaking process itself and the personal and creative challenges behind bringing stories to the screen,” the festival said in a release.

“Half a century after Rocky first reached audiences and the Cairo International Film Festival was founded, the opening night of CIFF’s 47th edition brings these two histories together: one celebrating the determination of a young actor who fought to bring his character to life, the other marking a cinematic journey that began in Cairo in 1976 and continues to connect audiences with films from around the world.”

The 47th edition will run November 11-20.

article_text:
Romanian filmmaker Cristian Mungiu is a card-carrying member of a very rare club as a two-time Cannes Film Festival Palme d’Or winner . Not only that, but he has won prizes at Cannes just about with every other film he chose to debut there. Those include his latest Fjord , which is not only Romania’s entry into the International Feature Film Oscar race (it qualifies even with the English language mixed with others), pundits have it as a good shot for a Best Picture and Director nomination among other categories.

Related Stories

Sebastian Stan On His Romanian Roots In ‘Fjord’, Fatherhood, Toxic Masculinity, Real-Life Heroes & ‘The Batman: Part II’ – Cannes Cover Story

‘Fjord’ DP Tudor Vladimir Panduru On Crafting Long Takes With Cristian Mungiu & Challenges Of Shooting In Remote Norway — ToruńCamerimage

This would be sweet because despite all the global acclaim Mungiu has yet to break in at the Oscars, most disappointedly after his first Palme d’Or winner, 2007’s 4 Months, 3 Weeks, And 2 Days , failed to make the cut — a shocker considering the critical support behind it. Other films like Beyond the Hills (2012) and Graduation (2016) and R.M.N. (2022) have kept him at the top of his game, returning him to Cannes every four years. But now it is Fjord , starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as a couple moving to Norway with five children and finding them at odds with local authorities over their parenting and religious beliefs, that is taking the filmmaker to a new level.

Watch on Deadline

Mungiu joins me this week for a new episode of my Deadline video series Behind the Lens where we talk about all of it, plus his hopes for Fjord, the seventh Palme d’Or winner in a row for its distributor Neon, at the Oscars. Just this past weekend it received five nominations at the European Film Awards and seems well on its way to the Dolby Theater in March.

To watch our conversation and go “behind the lens” with Cristian Mungiu, watch the video above.

Nos coups de cœur de la semaine, Léana Vigier et Luna Leblanc, mettent en avant les femmes . Les femmes sont belles, c’est une évidence, mais avec ces deux artistes leur beauté n’est pas ce qui a de plus intéressant à regarder. Elles sont fortes, mystérieuses, intrigantes et talentueuses. Elles nous regardent et n’ont pas peur de s’exprimer à travers l’appareil photo.

Léana Vigier

Comment faire une vraie ode à la féminité ? Léana Vigier se penche sur le sujet et cherche à créer, dans ses images, une proximité naturelle et contemplative entre deux femmes. Les clichés nous plongent dans un parc, un moment suspendu de la réalité où les deux filles sont seules au monde. La ville est endormie, les femmes semblent à nouveau libres et indépendantes ! Ici, la beauté n’a pas besoin de s’expliquer, la complicité est présente sans en dire trop. Pour nous expliquer son projet, l’artiste nous dit qu’elle porte une attention très particulière aux « regards et aux gestes des mains. Je trouve qu’ils racontent énormément de choses sur une relation, parfois bien plus que les mots » . Guidée par sa sensibilité, Léana Vigier photographie ce qui est simple et spontané pour rendre visibles « des détails auxquels on ne prête pas forcément attention » . À travers l’image, nous ressentons le silence qui relie les deux femmes dans l’intimité et une certaine union, ces photographies nous permettent de porter un regard attentif sur leurs visages et les émotions qui les traversent. Une relation se raconte avant tout par les gestes, les corps, les regards et la présence dans l’espace. « J’aime particulièrement figer les mouvements naturels du corps, les gestes spontanés et les attitudes qui ne sont pas réellement conscientes. Il y a quelque chose que je trouve très beau dans ces instants suspendus, presque cinématographiques, où l’on a l’impression que l’image appartient à une scène plus longue » , nous avoue-t-elle.

Luna Leblanc

« Je cherche à donner forme à l’univers qui existe dans mon esprit, un univers constitué de tout ce que j’observe, de ce que je rencontre et de ce que j’absorbe au fil de la vie. » Chez Luna Leblanc, chaque image est mise en scène, elle travaille la couleur et le noir et blanc pour que les clichés soient à la frontière entre le souvenir et le rêve. La personne photographiée prend un rôle, les femmes sont sublimées et nous apparaissent comme des fantômes qui nous interpellent. Les figures se dédoublent, parfois à travers un miroir, pour mettre en avant une partie du corps. Nous découvrons le corps en entier, d’abord les lèvres, la bouche entière, les yeux, le nez, mais aussi une femme nue se cachant derrière un rideau. Les images sont puissantes et dégagent un message clair, celui du pouvoir qui ressort de ces femmes. Pour créer, l’artiste nous confie qu’elle s’intéresse « aux procédés photographiques traditionnels, notamment à la solarisation, qu'[elle] réinterprète dans un flux de travail entièrement numérique » . Ce sont alors de poses longues où la lumière est continue accompagnée de flash pour explorer les différentes possibilités expressives de la luminosité et du mouvement. Dans sa photographie, Luna Leblanc retravaille tout pour réussir à créer une image intrigante qui incarne la beauté.

Die Monopol Top 100 in den Medien, Abschottung des Kunstmarktes und Reaktionen auf den neuen James Bond: Das ist unsere Presseschau am Dienstag

Monopol Top 100 Wir haben die neue Monopol Top 100 veröffentlicht, und viele andere Medien haben die Liste aufgegriffen. Chefredakteurin Elke Buhr lobt in der Sendung "Fazit" auf Deutschlandfunk Kultur die Nummer eins, die Choreografin Florentina Holzinger , deren Inszenierung des österreichischen Pavillons in Venedig die internationale Kunstwelt überrascht habe. Buhr über ihren unverstellten Blick auf den weiblichen Körper: "Der nackte weibliche Körper bei Florentina Holzinger ist nicht sexualisiert." Platz zwei belegt die Unesco – auch als politisches Bekenntnis zum Schutz des kulturellen Erbes angesichts autoritärer Kräfte. Die Liste sei bewusst zur Hälfte Künstlerinnen und Künstlern, zur anderen Hälfte den Ermöglicherinnen und Ermöglichern ihrer Arbeit gewidmet. Auch Naomi Beckwith, künstlerische Leiterin der kommenden Documenta, sei schon jetzt eine einflussreiche Figur. Außerdem war Elke Buhr in der WDR3-Sendung "Mosaik" und im SWR Kultur zu Gast, um über das Ranking zu sprechen.

Nicola Kuhn sieht im "Tagesspiegel" in der großen Zahl Berliner Namen in der Monopol Top 100 einen Beleg für die anhaltende internationale Bedeutung der Hauptstadt als Kunststandort. Sie hebt außerdem Kathleen Reinhardt ( hier im Monopol-Interview) hervor, die den deutschen Pavillon in Venedig verantwortete, sowie zahlreiche Berliner Museumsdirektoren und Kunstschaffende. Eine Überraschung am Ende der Liste ist für sie der Porträtist Jérémie Queyras, dessen Merkel-Bildnis ihm unverhoffte Aufmerksamkeit verschafft habe.

Kunstmarkt

Scott Reyburn stellt in der "Art Newspaper" die Frage, ob Kunstmessen überhaupt an Besuchern interessiert sind, die nicht zum Kreis der VIPs und potenziellen Käufer gehören. Die vorzeitige Schließung der Art Basel Paris nach der VIP-Preview habe ein deutliches Signal gesetzt, wie wenig Besucher, die lediglich Kunst sehen statt kaufen wollen, zählen. Reyburn kritisiert die zunehmende Abschottung des Kunstmarkts : Eintrittspreise von 47 Euro in Paris und 48 Pfund bei der Frieze in London machten Kunstmessen für junge und weniger wohlhabende Menschen kaum erschwinglich und dienten weniger der Einnahmengenerierung als der Exklusivität. Reyburn warnt, dass Kunstsammeln zunehmend als Hobby alter, reicher Menschen wahrgenommen werde, und fordert mehr Offenheit statt Abschottung.

KI

Tom Seymour untersucht im "Art Journal" , wie sich die Rolle künstlicher Intelligenz in der Kunst verändert: Maschinen erzeugen nicht mehr nur Bilder, sondern treffen zunehmend eigenständig Entscheidungen. An Beispielen von Paris Photo, Frieze und Art Basel zeigt er, wie Künstler KI als vermeintliche Kollaborateurin einsetzen. Besonders weit geht der Berliner Künstler Jonas Lund, dessen Installation "Performance Review" eine KI über die Produktion und Bewertung von Kunstwerken entscheiden lässt. Seymour warnt jedoch davor, die Systeme als autonome Akteure zu betrachten: Hinter ihnen stünden menschliche Entscheidungen, wirtschaftliche Interessen und enorme ökologische Ressourcen. "Unsere Systeme wurden von Menschen geschaffen, und die Entscheidungen über sie bleiben menschliche Entscheidungen", schreibt er. Die Kunst könne helfen, sichtbar zu machen, welche Kontrolle wir an Maschinen abgeben.

Malerei

Julian Bell würdigt in der "London Review of Books" anlässlich von Christopher Lloyds neuer Biografie des britischen Malers Michael Andrews als einen der großen, aber weniger bekannten Künstler des 20. Jahrhunderts. Andrews habe zunächst das ausschweifende Leben der Londoner Bohème und der internationalen Jetset-Gesellschaft festgehalten, sich später jedoch zunehmend existenziellen und allegorischen Themen zugewandt. Bell beschreibt einen Künstler, dessen Werk sich keiner einheitlichen Handschrift unterordne und der sich zeitlebens mit dem Gefühl des Fremdseins auseinandergesetzt habe. Gerade diese Unruhe habe seinen Blick geschärft: "Er war ständig aufmerksam, weil er ständig ängstlich war." Andrews' Malerei stelle, so Bell, eine ebenso große Herausforderung dar wie alles andere in der britischen Kunst des 20. Jahrhunderts.

Film

Robert Pattinson wird der neue James Bond . "Pattinson war eine sichere Wahl: gutaussehend, weiß, britisch, erprobt in Mega-Filmreihen und jemand, der bereits bei 'Dune: Part Three' mit (Regisseur Denis) Villeneuve zusammengearbeitet hat", kommentiert die "New York Times" . "Und trotzdem deutet so gut wie nichts in Pattinsons bisheriger Karriere darauf hin, dass er ein konventioneller Bond sein wird. Er spielt gerne mit der Demontage männlicher Selbstsicherheit und der Verkörperung von Männern voller Unsicherheiten oder moralischer Schwächen." Das "Aftonbladet" meint: "Es wurde keine Verjüngung, wie lange spekuliert wurde. Aber die Wahl von Robert Pattinson als neuer James Bond ist smart, allein schon, weil er bereits ein großer Star ist, auf den Amazon offensichtlich setzt, um ein großes Publikum anzulocken. Es hilft natürlich, dass er eine ewig junge Aura besitzt, dass er immer noch als der Emo-Typ betrachtet wird, auch wenn sein Durchbruch mit den 'Twilight'-Filmen schon viele Jahre her ist. Wir betrachten ihn jedenfalls nicht als 40-Jährigen." Für "Libération" zeigt Amazon eine "gewisse verständliche Nervosität", "indem es auf die Sicherheit eines in Hollywood sehr bekannten Schauspielers setzt, dessen Wandelbarkeit unbestritten ist und oft gelobt wurde." "Paris Match" sieht in Pattinson einen neuer Männertypus James Bond verkörpert: "Elegant, raffiniert, dunkel ... Vielleicht ermöglicht das, Schluss mit dem langjährigen unverschämten Machismus dieser Rolle zu machen. Nach Jahren der Gerüchte stellt die Wahl von Robert Pattinson Filmliebhaber und das breite Publikum zufrieden, die Verfechter einer gewissen Klassik wie jene, die eine Auffrischung des Mythos wollen. Auf gewisse Weise ist es eine ideale Wahl."

article_text:
Starting November 25, or the day before Thanksgiving in the US and two days before Black Friday, Christie’s will offer a collection of some 100 rare Louis Vuitton handbags, featuring collaborations with artists like Takashi Murakami , Frank Gehry , and Yayoi Kusama . The “Scarcity & Infinity” sale will be offered online during the house’s luxury week from November 25 to December 10, with a selection of handbags on view at Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters from December 3–9.

“This collection celebrates an extraordinary intersection of art, fashion, and design, and the idea that a work of art can be something we carry with us,” Rachel Koffsky Parker, Christie’s international head of handbags and accessories, said in a statement.

Highlights include several examples from Murakami’s many Artycapucines collaborations with Louis Vuitton, from a Swarovski crystal-encrusted grinning, wide-eyed panda purse (estimated at $20,000–$30,000) to a semicircular bag covered with rainbow mink fur ($10,000–$15,000) to a pink calfskin handbag covered with octopus tentacles ($10,000–$15,000). The Swarovski panda is the sale’s top lot.

“Scarcity & Infinity” also includes a limited-edition yellow leather pumpkin-shaped bag designed by Kusama in 2023; here, her trademark polka dots are replaced by black LV logos.

Both Kusama and Murakami have long histories of collaboration with Louis Vuitton, but that is not as much the case with another designer included in the sale. The late architect Frank Gehry , known for his sweeping, shimmering designs for museums like the Guggenheim Bilbao and the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, notably worked with the fashion house in 2023 on a line of 11 handbags that were presented at Art Basel Miami Beach that year. Several of those bags, including a metallic bear ($10,000–$15,000) and a white crocodile Capucines bag emblazoned with a red fish ($6,000–$8,000), are also part of the sale.

Handbags from other artist collaborations that will be offered by Christie’s include ones by Pharrell Williams, Stephen Sprouse, Jeff Koons, Nigel Peake, Tom Sachs, and Yohei Yama.

article_text:
FLECHA 1

O CORAÇÃO DE UMA SERPENTE repousando confortavelmente em meu dorso, ela entregou uma parte da floresta que eu temia, ou não ousaria me aproximar. toda caçadora precisa, antes de mais nada, criar intimidade com suas curvas o ritmo do seu coração tranquilo ainda orquestra os meus passos.

FLECHA 2

O SOL DE DENTRO vejo um imenso sol no centro do peito de todas as pessoas que encontrei aqui seus corpos escuros ondulam-se como os da minha terra agarram o tempo sem afobação os assobios dos pássaros se entrelaçam ao canto de uma mulher.

FLECHA 3

A SABEDORIA MILENAR DE UM FÓSSIL meia-noite aqui, o céu é sépia, flutuo meu corpo molhado sobre esta paisagem, uma antiga aldeia submersa não há nada que possa revelar melhor sua estória do que dançar com as suas ruínas então, ao som das risadas de suas mulheres, eu danço.

FLECHA 4

OFÁ o arco que devolve ao chão a verdadeira nobreza, como na obra de Abdias do Nascimento.

FLECHA 5

À NOSSA MÃE entre as nuvens, entre as águas, sendo ela a própria kalunga a porta de entrada do mundo: mãe com coragem nos deu a mão e nos levou para passear no impossível, e aqui estamos.

FLECHA 6

A MÁSCARA um fractal de rostos e olhares, milhares à frente, milhares atrás de nós a máscara alarga o nosso espírito nos coloca à disposição do tempo assombra os nossos inimigos.

FLECHA 7

KINTSUGI a rachadura sempre fará parte da nossa estória não é algo possível de restaurar ela é irreparável mas a verdade é que no invisível ela nunca existiu.

FLECHA 8

OSÙN a água é sempre subversiva.

FLECHA 9

MARIA DO CARMO o que sonhava minha avó? o que de seu sonho perpetua minha existência? fecho os olhos a fim de decifrar esta memória irreparável ao redor de mim mesma o que me conecta a ela e ao que sou? quero parecer-me com ela que nunca vi reencontrar as impressões de suas lembranças enquanto danço.

FLECHA 10

“às vezes voltar e seguir em frente coincidem.” (Saidiya Hartman)

FLECHA 11

ADUBAR O CÉU lembre-se de: cantar uma mesma canção por muitas vidas adubar o céu, conversar com os buritis, envelhecer.

FLECHA 12

SONHAR É UMA MUSCULATURA sonhar é uma musculatura sonhar é uma musculatura

O AZUL QUE MORA EM MIM ,

colocar as mãos dentro de uma tina de índigo, tocando a água, e observar um tecido completamente branco transformar-se em azul. esse mesmo tecido, ao receber os primeiros raios de sol, escalará uma paleta de tons em sua divina metamorfose, até assentar seu imprevisível contorno ultramarino, cobalto ou prússia, quase sempre do mais negro até a cor do céu em um dia de verão. depois da etapa final, o azul seguirá diluindo-se, espalhando-se na pele, impregnando tudo o que estiver a seu redor, insistindo em surgir, mesmo com a certeza de que desaparecerá.

a cianotipia me levou para a mesma jornada em direção ao desaparecimento. mais um tempo encharcado e fecundo. e esses azuis, generosamente, têm me libertado , por serem subversivos como a água, por irem me afundando junto com as minhas mãos em sua poesia radical, lançando-me na recusa de não lembrar apenas da dor; de querer permanecer na poesia, na alquimia do gesto e na escuridão solar, familiar, perene de meus ancestrais.

em Doze flechas feitas de água (2026), véus penderão como corpos movendo-se com o ar, e ao redor deles um som prolongará esse convite para habitarmos aquilo que escapa aos olhos e encontra abrigo na escuta. o que desaparece continua vibrando na frequência das águas, das vozes e das presenças que esse azul convoca, como o índigo que insiste em retornar à nossa pele negra, ou como o mar que nunca termina de chegar à margem.

mais do que superfícies, tecidos são memórias encarnadas, guardam histórias, anunciam pertencimentos, carregam conhecimentos espirituais e preservam mundos inteiros em suas tramas. como o corpo, acumulam camadas, absorvem o tempo, são marcados, dobrados, tingidos, remendados e transformados, e cada fibra torna-se testemunha de um encontro entre matéria, gesto e duração. talvez por isso a gente tenha escolhido tantas etapas, o filme analógico, a cianotipia, para depois suspender essas imagens azuis sobre tecidos quase transparentes. queríamos ver todos esses tempos orbitando em comum acordo, como peles que respiram e se misturam, irrigando lugares onde a memória continua nos sustentando, entre aparição e desaparecimento, entre arquivo e sonho.

criamos flechas que são como provérbios, pequenas sentenças lançadas em espirais capazes de atravessar distâncias que um corpo sozinho não alcança. cada uma delas carrega uma lembrança, uma orí entação, apontando para a possibilidade de derivar, mais uma vez, pelas ruas do benin, pelo chão da floresta sagrada de kpassè, pelo mar de salvador, ou entre os tecidos dispostos ao sol na ilha de tchiakpè-codji. essas flechas são feitas de água porque recusam as fronteiras, escolhem o movimento, sabem que a kalunga continua sendo nosso principal elo de ligação.

cada flecha é uma tentativa de honrar aquilo que permanece vivo entre uma margem e outra. doze flechas em uma dança de confiança.

INAÊ MOREIRA ///
